subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: As-salaamu alaykum, and welcome to your first Year 4 Science unit! In this unit you are going to become a living things detective. Everywhere you look, from the busy market in Mogadishu to the wide golden savanna near Garissa, you are surrounded by living things. There are goats chewing acacia leaves, weaver birds building nests, tilapia darting through the Jubba River, and tiny ants marching across the ground carrying crumbs bigger than their own bodies. In this unit you will learn how scientists make sense of all this life by sorting living things into groups, and how every plant and animal is perfectly suited to the place it calls home.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Know that humans (and some animals) have bony skeletons inside their bodies
Investigate how different animals are found in different habitats and are suited to the environment in which they are found

objectives.subStrand: Obtain and present evidence; Consider evidence and approach
objectives.text: Make relevant observations and comparisons in a variety of contexts

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to do all of the following. Keep this list nearby and tick each one off when you feel confident.
Explain the difference between living, once-living, and non-living things, and name the seven signs of life.
Sort living things into the two big kingdoms you will study: plants and animals.
Explain what a vertebrate and an invertebrate are, and give examples of each.
Name and describe the five groups of vertebrates: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.
Describe the main groups of plants, including flowering plants and non-flowering plants.
Use a simple classification key to identify an animal by answering yes-or-no questions.
Build and explain a food chain, using the words producer, consumer, predator, and prey.
Explain what a habitat is and describe several East African habitats such as savanna, desert, and mangrove.
Explain how living things show adaptations that help them survive in their habitat.

concepts.title: Is It Living, Once-Living, or Non-Living?
concepts.explanation:
Before we can sort living things into groups, we must first answer a simpler question: what makes something alive? This sounds easy, but it can be tricky. A rushing river moves and a flickering fire grows, yet neither is alive. Meanwhile, a seed sitting still in the dry ground looks like it is doing nothing, yet it is very much alive. So how do scientists decide?

Scientists use a checklist of seven signs of life. If something does all seven, it is living. A helpful way to remember them is that all living things move, breathe, sense, grow, feed, get rid of waste, and reproduce (make young). Let us walk through them one by one, using animals and plants you know.

Movement — Living things can move by themselves. A goat walks, a bird flies, and even a sunflower slowly turns to face the sun.

Breathing (respiration) — Living things take in the gases they need to release energy from their food. A camel breathes air; a tilapia takes in oxygen from water through its gills.

Sensing — Living things notice and respond to the world. A gazelle hears a lion and runs; a plant's roots grow toward water.

Growth — Living things grow bigger and change. A tiny acacia seed grows into a huge thorny tree; a calf grows into a full-grown cow.

Feeding (nutrition) — Living things need food for energy. Animals eat other living things; plants make their own food from sunlight.

Getting rid of waste (excretion) — Living things remove the waste their bodies make, just as you do when you breathe out or visit the toilet.

Reproduction — Living things make more of their own kind. Camels have calves, birds lay eggs, and plants make seeds.

Now think about a rock. It never grows on its own, never feeds, never has babies. It is non-living. Think about a wooden stool or a piece of dried frankincense resin. It was once part of a living tree, but it is no longer alive. We call these things once-living. And a leather sandal, made from an animal's skin, is once-living too. Learning to tell these three groups apart is the very first skill of a living things detective.
concepts.example: Did You Know? A date palm seed can stay alive but resting for many years. Scientists once grew a healthy date palm from a 2,000-year-old seed found in the desert!

concepts.title: The Big Groups - Plants and Animals
concepts.explanation:
Once we know something is alive, the next question is: what kind of living thing is it? Scientists sort all living things into large groups called kingdoms. There are several kingdoms, including tiny living things too small to see, but in Year 4 we will focus on the two you know best: the plant kingdom and the animal kingdom.

The clearest difference between plants and animals is how they get their food. Plants make their own food. Using their green leaves, sunlight, water, and a gas from the air called carbon dioxide, plants make sugar in a process called photosynthesis. Because plants make food, we call them producers. Think of the acacia trees and grasses of the savanna, or the mango and banana trees in a garden in Kismaayo. They are food factories powered by the sun.

Animals cannot make their own food. They must eat other living things to get energy. A cow eats grass, a lion eats a gazelle, and a person eats bariis (rice), goat meat, and dates. Because animals eat other living things, we call them consumers. Animals also usually move around to find their food, and most have sense organs like eyes and ears to help them. Plants, in contrast, usually stay rooted in one place.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Every breath of oxygen you take was made by a plant or by tiny plant-like living things in the ocean. Without plants, animals could not breathe.

concepts.title: Animals With Backbones and Without
concepts.explanation:
The animal kingdom is huge, so scientists split it in two. Stand up straight and reach behind you to feel the middle of your back. Can you feel the row of little bumps running from your neck down to your waist? That is your backbone, also called your spine. It is made of many small bones and it holds your body up.

Animals that have a backbone are called vertebrates. Animals that do not have a backbone are called invertebrates. This one feature divides the whole animal kingdom into two enormous camps. A lion, a camel, a flamingo, a crocodile, and a tilapia are all vertebrates, like you. An ant, a spider, a snail, a butterfly, and an earthworm are all invertebrates.

Here is something surprising. Even though the big animals we notice first, like elephants and giraffes, are vertebrates, the truth is that most animals on Earth are invertebrates. For every vertebrate, there are many, many invertebrates. Think of how many ants live in a single savanna, or how many mosquitoes buzz near a pond. Invertebrates are the hidden majority of the animal world.
concepts.example: Invertebrates come in many shapes. Some, like beetles, ants, and grasshoppers, are insects with six legs and a hard outer covering. Spiders and scorpions have eight legs. Snails have soft bodies and often a shell. Worms have long, soft, boneless bodies. None of them has a backbone, which is exactly why they can be so small and so many.

concepts.title: The Five Groups of Vertebrates
concepts.explanation:
All vertebrates share a backbone, but they are not all the same. Scientists sort vertebrates into five groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Each group has its own set of clues that help you recognise it. Learn these clues well, because you will use them to become a fast, confident classifier.

Fish live in water their whole lives. They breathe using gills, which take in oxygen straight from the water, so they do not need to come up for air the way you do. Their bodies are usually covered in scales, and they swim using fins and a strong tail. Fish are cold-blooded, which means their body warms up or cools down with the water around them. The tilapia and Nile perch that swim in the Jubba River, and the many fish caught along the Indian Ocean coast, are all fish.

Amphibians, such as frogs and toads, live part of their life in water and part on land. Their name even means 'two lives'. They have smooth, moist skin with no scales. Baby frogs, called tadpoles, hatch in water and breathe with gills like fish. As they grow, they develop legs and lungs and can hop onto land. Amphibians are cold-blooded and lay their soft eggs in water, such as the ponds and swamps that fill up during the rainy season.

Reptiles, such as snakes, lizards, crocodiles, and tortoises, have dry, scaly skin. Unlike amphibians, their skin does not need to stay wet, so many reptiles do very well in hot, dry places like the semi-arid land of the Horn of Africa. Reptiles are cold-blooded, so you will often see a lizard basking on a warm rock in the morning sun to heat up its body. Most reptiles lay eggs with tough, leathery shells on land. The Nile crocodile resting on a riverbank is a famous African reptile.

Birds are the only animals with feathers. All birds have two wings, two legs, and a beak instead of teeth, and they lay hard-shelled eggs. Most birds can fly, though a few, like the ostrich, cannot. Birds are warm-blooded, which means their bodies stay at a steady warm temperature no matter how cold or hot it is outside. East Africa is full of wonderful birds: pink flamingos wading in the salty Rift Valley lakes, weaver birds stitching their hanging nests, and eagles circling high above the plains.

Mammals are the group you belong to. Mammals have hair or fur on their bodies, they are warm-blooded, and mother mammals feed their babies milk from their own bodies. Most mammals give birth to live young rather than laying eggs. The savanna is full of mammals: lions, elephants, giraffes, and camels, as well as the goats, cattle, and donkeys that families keep. And of course, you are a mammal too.

Here is a table to gather all five groups in one place. Study it, then try to picture one animal from each group in your mind.
concepts.example: Did You Know? A flamingo is pink because of the tiny shrimp and algae it eats in the Rift Valley lakes. A flamingo that eats different food turns pale! A whale lives in the sea but is not a fish. It is a mammal that breathes air and feeds its baby milk, just like a camel.

concepts.title: The Groups of Plants
concepts.explanation:
Just as animals are sorted into groups, so are plants. The simplest way to sort plants is by asking one question: does it make flowers?

Flowering plants grow flowers, and their flowers turn into fruits that hold seeds. Most of the plants you eat and see every day are flowering plants: the mango, banana, and papaya trees in a garden, the grasses of the savanna, the acacia with its tiny puffball flowers, and the mighty baobab tree. The flower's job is to help the plant make seeds so that new plants can grow.

Non-flowering plants never make flowers. Instead they make new plants in other ways, often by making tiny dust-like spores. Ferns, which love damp shady corners, and mosses, which form soft green cushions on wet rocks and walls, are non-flowering plants. They are usually smaller and prefer wetter places.

Most flowering plants share the same three main parts, and each part has a job. Learning these parts helps you understand how a plant lives.

Roots hold the plant firmly in the ground and drink up water and minerals from the soil. A baobab's roots spread wide to catch every drop of rare rain.

Stem holds the plant up and carries water from the roots to the leaves, like pipes carrying water through a house.

Leaves are the plant's food factories. They catch sunlight and make food through photosynthesis.
concepts.example: Flowers make seeds so the plant can reproduce, and their fruits protect and carry those seeds.

concepts.title: Sorting With a Classification Key
concepts.explanation:
Scientists have a clever tool for identifying living things called a classification key, or sometimes a 'branching key'. It works by asking a series of yes-or-no questions. Each answer sends you down a different path, until you arrive at the name of your animal. It is a bit like a game of twenty questions.

Imagine you find an animal and want to know which vertebrate group it belongs to. You could follow a key like this:

Does it have hair or fur and feed its babies milk? If yes, it is a mammal. If no, go to question 2.

Does it have feathers? If yes, it is a bird. If no, go to question 3.

Does it live in water and breathe with gills its whole life? If yes, it is a fish. If no, go to question 4.

Does it have dry, scaly skin and lay leathery eggs on land? If yes, it is a reptile. If no, it is most likely an amphibian.

Let us test it with a camel. Question 1: Does it have hair and feed its babies milk? Yes! So a camel is a mammal, and we did not even need the other questions. Now try a crocodile. Question 1: hair and milk? No. Question 2: feathers? No. Question 3: gills in water its whole life? No, it breathes air. Question 4: dry scaly skin and leathery eggs on land? Yes! So a crocodile is a reptile. Do you see how the key guides you step by step to the right answer?
concepts.example: [*] Remember! A good classification key uses clear yes-or-no questions about things you can actually see, like skin, legs, or feathers. Follow the key one question at a time. Never skip ahead, or you may end up at the wrong answer.

methods.title: The Living Things Hunt
methods.example: To observe and sort the living, once-living, and non-living things around your home.
steps: Draw a table on your paper with three columns: Living, Once-living, and Non-living.
Walk slowly around your home and garden with an adult.
Each time you spot something, decide which column it belongs in and write it down.
For each living thing, quickly note whether it is a plant or an animal.
Try to find at least five things for each column.

methods.title: Sorting the Animals (Classification Key)
methods.example: To build and use your own classification key to sort animals into the five vertebrate groups.
steps: On your paper, write the five group names: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.
Think of at least twelve animals you know, including local ones like camel, goat, tilapia, flamingo, crocodile, lizard, and frog.
For each animal, ask the key questions: Does it have hair and feed milk? Feathers? Gills in water? Dry scales and leathery eggs? Then place it in the right group.
Now write your own three-question key that a friend could follow to sort any animal.
Test your key by asking a family member to use it on an animal you choose.

methods.title: How a Camel's Fat Keeps It Going (Water and Storage)
methods.example: To model how storing something (like fat in a camel's hump) helps an animal survive when supplies run low.
steps: Fill both cups with the same amount of water and mark the level on the outside of each.
Leave one cup open. Cover the second cup loosely with the cloth or saucer.
Place both cups on a warm, sunny windowsill.
Each day for three days, mark the new water level in each cup.
Compare how much water is left in each cup after three days.

methods.title: Do Plants Reach for the Light?
methods.example: To observe whether a plant responds to light, showing that plants are alive and sense their environment.
steps: If using seeds, plant two or three beans in a cup of soil and water them lightly. If using a potted plant, simply use it as it is.
Place the cup or pot on a windowsill so that light comes mainly from one side.
Water the soil a little each day to keep it damp, not soaked.
Each day for one week, look at the direction the stem and leaves are pointing and draw what you see.
After a few days, turn the plant around so the light comes from the other side, and keep watching.

methods.title: Build a Savanna Food Chain
methods.example: To build and explain food chains using living things from a habitat near you.
steps: On separate small cards, write or draw these living things: grass, gazelle, lion, grasshopper, lizard, eagle, acacia tree, and the sun.
Arrange the cards to make a food chain, placing the sun and a plant first.
Draw arrows between the cards. Remember: each arrow points from the food to the eater.
Now make a second, different food chain using the same cards in a new order where it makes sense.
Label each card as a producer, a consumer, a predator, or prey.

workedExamples.title: Classifying an Unknown Animal
workedExamples.prompt: Let us work through a full example together, step by step, just like a scientist would. Imagine your cousin Yusuf describes an animal he saw near the river: 'It had dry scaly skin, four short legs, it laid leathery eggs on the sandy bank, and it warmed itself in the morning sun.' What is it?
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Vertebrate or invertebrate? It has legs and a solid body with a backbone shape, and later we hear it is large and strong. It is a vertebrate.

Step 2 — Use the key. Hair and milk? No mention of fur, and reptiles do not feed milk. So it is not a mammal.

Step 3 — Feathers? No feathers are described. So it is not a bird.

Step 4 — Gills in water for its whole life? No, it comes onto the sandy bank and suns itself. So it is not a fish.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: An animal with a backbone is called a: (a) invertebrate (b) vertebrate (c) producer (d) predator
workedExamples.solution: (b) vertebrate. A vertebrate is an animal with a backbone, or spine.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is an invertebrate? (a) camel (b) tilapia (c) ant (d) flamingo
workedExamples.solution: (c) ant. An ant has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate. The others are all vertebrates.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Which vertebrate group has feathers? (a) mammals (b) reptiles (c) birds (d) fish
workedExamples.solution: (c) birds. Feathers are found only on birds; no other animal group has them.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: A camel belongs to which vertebrate group? (a) reptiles (b) mammals (c) birds (d) amphibians
workedExamples.solution: (b) mammals. A camel has hair and feeds its young milk, which are mammal features.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a producer? (a) lion (b) gazelle (c) acacia tree (d) eagle
workedExamples.solution: (c) acacia tree. A plant makes its own food from sunlight, so it is a producer.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: In the food chain grass -> gazelle -> lion, the lion is the: (a) producer (b) prey (c) predator (d) plant
workedExamples.solution: (c) predator. The lion hunts and eats the gazelle, so it is the predator.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: A frog that lives partly in water and partly on land is a: (a) fish (b) amphibian (c) reptile (d) bird
workedExamples.solution: (b) amphibian. Amphibians such as frogs live partly in water and partly on land.

practice.prompt: A habitat is best described as: (a) a type of food (b) the natural home of a living thing (c) a group of bones (d) a kind of plant
practice.answer: (b) the natural home of a living thing. A habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space.

practice.prompt: The camel's hump is an example of a: (a) food chain (b) predator (c) habitat (d) adaptation
practice.answer: (d) adaptation. The hump is a body feature that helps the camel survive in the desert.

practice.prompt: Which animal is a reptile? (a) frog (b) crocodile (c) flamingo (d) tilapia

practice.prompt: Plants make their own food using sunlight in a process called: (a) migration (b) photosynthesis (c) classification (d) reproduction
practice.answer: (b) photosynthesis. This is how green plants make food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide.

Place both cups on a warm, sunny windowsill.
Each day for three days, mark the new water level in each cup.
Compare how much water is left in each cup after three days.

activities.title: Do Plants Reach for the Light?
activities.materials: A few dried beans or maize seeds, or a small potted plant you already have; A cup or small pot with soil; Water; A window that gets sunlight from one side
steps: If using seeds, plant two or three beans in a cup of soil and water them lightly. If using a potted plant, simply use it as it is.
Place the cup or pot on a windowsill so that light comes mainly from one side.
Water the soil a little each day to keep it damp, not soaked.
Each day for one week, look at the direction the stem and leaves are pointing and draw what you see.
After a few days, turn the plant around so the light comes from the other side, and keep watching.

activities.title: Build a Savanna Food Chain
activities.materials: Paper and pencil, or small pieces of paper (cards); Coloured pencils if you have them
steps: On separate small cards, write or draw these living things: grass, gazelle, lion, grasshopper, lizard, eagle, acacia tree, and the sun.
Arrange the cards to make a food chain, placing the sun and a plant first.
Draw arrows between the cards. Remember: each arrow points from the food to the eater.
Now make a second, different food chain using the same cards in a new order where it makes sense.
Label each card as a producer, a consumer, a predator, or prey.

activities.title: Observe: Sorting With a Classification Key
activities.materials: A pencil and paper or notebook; A safe area to walk around, such as your home, yard, or garden; An adult to walk with you
steps: Look for an example of sorting with a classification key around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Group and Fish.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Is It Living, Once-Living, or Non-Living?
rules.text: Before we can sort living things into groups, we must first answer a simpler question: what makes something alive?

rules.title: The Big Groups — Plants and Animals
rules.text: Once we know something is alive, the next question is: what kind of living thing is it?

rules.title: Animals With Backbones and Without
rules.text: The animal kingdom is huge, so scientists split it in two.

rules.title: The Five Groups of Vertebrates
rules.text: All vertebrates share a backbone, but they are not all the same.

rules.title: The Groups of Plants
rules.text: Just as animals are sorted into groups, so are plants.

rules.title: Sorting With a Classification Key

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the main difference between a vertebrate and an invertebrate?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A vertebrate has a backbone (spine) inside its body; an invertebrate has no backbone. This is the key difference.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the five groups of vertebrates.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The five groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how plants and animals get their food differently.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Plants make their own food from sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide through photosynthesis, so they are producers. Animals cannot make food and must eat other living things, so they are consumers.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is an adaptation? Give one example from an East African animal.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: An adaptation is a body feature or behaviour that helps a living thing survive in its habitat. Example: a camel's hump stores fat for energy and water in the dry desert (other correct examples include the giraffe's long neck or the elephant's trunk).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must every food chain begin with a plant?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because plants are the only producers; they capture the sun's energy and make food. Without a plant at the start, there would be no energy entering the chain for animals to use.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name three different habitats found in East Africa.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any three of: savanna, desert or semi-arid land, mangrove swamp, river, coral reef (other reasonable East African habitats are also acceptable).

rounds.explanation: ant. An ant has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate. The others are all vertebrates.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a producer?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: acacia tree. A plant makes its own food from sunlight, so it is a producer.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the seven signs of life?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: being made of metal. Metal is not a sign of life. The seven signs include growing, feeding, and reproducing.

games.title: Unit Champion: Fish
games.description: Practise fish through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Plants make their own food using sunlight in a process called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: photosynthesis. This is how green plants make food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide.

rounds.prompt: Which vertebrate group has feathers?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: birds. Feathers are found only on birds; no other animal group has them.

rounds.prompt: In the food chain grass -> gazelle -> lion, the lion is the:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: predator. The lion hunts and eats the gazelle, so it is the predator.

rounds.prompt: A habitat is best described as:
choices: the natural home of a living thing
rounds.answer: the natural home of a living thing
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 1 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: the natural home of a living thing. A habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to do all of the following. Keep this list nearby and tick each one off when you feel confident.
I can explain the difference between living, once-living, and non-living things, and name the seven signs of life.
I can sort living things into the two big kingdoms you will study: plants and animals.
I can explain what a vertebrate and an invertebrate are, and give examples of each.
I can name and describe the five groups of vertebrates: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.
I can describe the main groups of plants, including flowering plants and non-flowering plants.
I can use a simple classification key to identify an animal by answering yes-or-no questions.
I can build and explain a food chain, using the words producer, consumer, predator, and prey.
